newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania risks hyper inflation after savings scam.
newsitem.headline: Albania risks hyper inflation after savings scam.

text.p: The Albanian government has promised to repay all unwary investors who have lost a fortune in crumbling pyramid savings schemes, but it risks unleashing hyper inflation if keeps its word, analysts said on Tuesday.
Economists believe Albanians might have plunged more than $1.0 billion into countless private funds which sprung up across the country following the demise of the old communist ruling elite in 1990.

At least five of the top schemes have now hit the rocks and the rightist government has frozen bank assets from two of the funds worth around $300 million. Other pyramids are still operating but only paying interest, not returning capital.

"The seized money won't cover more than a third of the total amount invested in the schemes," said Zef Preci, director of the independent Albania Centre for Economic Research. "The only way the government can compensate people in full is by printing money and that will set inflation alight," he added.
Inflation dipped to around six percent in early 1996 but jumped to 17.4 percent year-on-year by December, hurt by a yawning government budget deficit.
Any further surge in prices could be ruinous for Europe's poorest economy and should be avoided at all costs, said Carlos Elbirt, the World Bank's resident representative in Tirana.
"Where is the money going to come from to pay back these people?" Elbirt told Reuters. "There is not the money in the state budget and printing money would mean hyper inflation."

According to latest data, the budget deficit in the first 11 months of 1996 hit around $260 million -- some 11 percent of gross domestic product, while the central bank has foreign exchange reserves of just $270 million.

To make matters harder for Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi as he seeks to keep his full repayment pledge, much of the frozen assets belonging to the two funds are held in the form of Albanian treasury bills.
Desperate investors, who went on the rampage last weekend in a wave of violent protests across the country, want hard cash and not government bonds.

In a bid to avoid further bloody clashes, the government will be anxious to satisfy their demands, but Elbirt thought the most people could hope for would be partial compensation, and urged Meksi to hold talks with all Albania's political forces to strike a cross-party deal over the crisis.

One glimmer of hope for the government might come from abroad with bodies like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and European Union unlikely to let the small Balkan state sink into economic chaos.
Such a crisis could unleash the sort of mass immigration seen in 1991 when tens of thousands of people tried to enter Greece and Italy illegally in a spectacular exodus.
The IMF resident representative in Albania, John King, told Reuters on Tuesday that the Washington-based group was ready to do "everything" that it could to help the Albanian government.
But foreign agencies cannot be expected to write a blank cheque to a government which opposition parties accuse of using the pyramid schemes to fund its 1996 general and local election campaigns.
Instead they would want a commitment that state accounts would be cleaned up and all the pyramid schemes cleared out.
"It is going to be a painful and costly process," the World Bank's Elbirt warned.
